# Don't replace your phone. Replace its ROM.

Old phone feeling slow, and no more updates? A custom ROM swaps the software your phone came with for a newer Android, without the maker's extra apps. It's free and built by the community. Search your phone to see what still builds for it.

Search by model name or codename. Searching sweet finds the Xiaomi Redmi Note 10 Pro.

...

## How to use this site

Four steps from the phone in your hand to a newer Android. Each step opens the page that helps with it.

1. Search your phone

Type the name, the model number or the codename. The codename is the safest match, because one model name can mean different hardware in different countries.
2. Pick a ROM that still builds for it

Your phone's page lists every project with a current build, the Android version each one runs and when it was last built. Builds a project stopped updating are listed apart.
3. Read the install guide

Back up first. Then unlock the bootloader, install a recovery and flash the ROM. The guide walks you through each step.
4. Download from the project itself

Every download link goes to the project's own site, checked against a list of official hosts. Nothing is reuploaded here.

...

What is a custom ROM?

A replacement Android build made by an independent project for specific phones. It can bring a newer Android version, fewer preinstalled apps or extra privacy features, often on phones the manufacturer no longer updates. What each build includes, and how often it updates, differs from project to project.

Title: Custom ROMs vs Stock Android 16: Still Worth It?
URL: https://thecustomrom.com/blog/custom-roms-vs-stock-android-16
Published: 2026-02-21T00:00:00.000Z
Author: N/A
Highlights:
### Camera

Let’s get the biggest one out of the way. Stock camera processing, especially on Pixel, Samsung, and OnePlus devices, is significantly better than custom ROMs. GCam ports help, but they’re never quite as good as the OEM’s optimized pipeline.

If photography matters to you, stock wins. Period.

### Convenience

- OTA updates just work
- No bootloader unlocking
- No risk of bricking
- Warranty stays intact
- Banking apps work without tricks
- Google Pay works out of the box

### Integration

Google’s own features need no setup on stock. Assistant, Circle to Search and Live Translate work best, and some work only, on stock Android with Google Play Services built into the system.

### Support

When something breaks on stock, you call the manufacturer. When something breaks on a custom ROM, you’re scrolling through Telegram groups at 2 AM looking for someone who had the same issue.

### Customization

Stock Android 16 gives you wallpaper-based theming and that’s about it. Custom ROMs like crDroid or Evolution X give you far more toggles than stock, custom status bars, gesture controls, font engines, and system-level changes that stock will never offer.

### Performance on Old Devices

A three-year-old phone on a lightweight custom ROM like LineageOS runs circles around the same phone struggling under OEM bloat. If your manufacturer has stopped updating your device, custom ROMs are the only way to get security patches and modern Android features.

### Privacy

Stock Android sends telemetry to Google constantly. Even with privacy settings tightened, Google collects location history, usage patterns, and device information. Custom ROMs without Google apps, or privacy-focused ones like GrapheneOS, cut most of it out. See our privacy ROMs comparison.

...

Recent Pixels and Samsung flagships now get seven years of updates (Google’s Pixel update schedule covers the Pixel 8 and later), but many budget phones still get two to four. Custom ROMs can keep a phone going after that, for as long as a maintainer keeps building for it. The Pixel 3, for example, runs Android 15 through LineageOS, crDroid and Evolution X, years after Google stopped updating it: its LineageOS wiki page lists LineageOS 22.2, based on Android 15, as the current version. (An earlier version of this article said Android 16; no official Android 16 build exists for it.)

...

## The Honest Breakdown

Neither side wins outright, so the table says what each one actually gives you rather than scoring it. Stock wins wherever the maker’s own software or Google’s checks matter: the camera pipeline, payments, banking apps and support. A custom ROM wins wherever control matters: what runs on the phone, how it looks, and how long it keeps getting updates. Performance is the closest call, because on the same phone it depends more on the maintainer’s kernel and the vendor files a ROM uses than on whether the system is stock or custom. On app compatibility, Google’s Play Integrity verdict documentation says the device integrity verdict on Android 13 and later needs hardware-backed proof of a locked bootloader running a certified manufacturer image:

| Category | Stock Android 16 | Custom ROM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Camera | The maker’s own camera app and image processing | A basic AOSP camera app; GCam ports help on some phones |
| Convenience | Automatic updates, no unlocking, warranty intact | Unlocked bootloader, firmware checks, updates you install yourself or through the ROM’s updater |
| Customization | Wallpaper colours, themed icons and, from QPR2, icon shapes | Status bar, Quick Settings, gestures and fonts, depending on the ROM |
| Privacy | Google services built in; settings limit collection but do not stop it | Can run with no Google apps, or with GrapheneOS’s sandboxed Google Play |
| Performance | Tuned by the maker for the hardware | Depends on the maintainer and the vendor files |
| Software support duration | Ends with the maker’s update window: seven years on recent Pixels and Samsung flagships, two to four on many budget phones | Lasts as long as a maintainer keeps building for the device |
| App compatibility | Passes Play Integrity, so banking and payment apps work | On Android 13 and later an unlocked bootloader fails Play Integrity’s device and strong checks, and some banking apps refuse to run |
| Learning curve | None | Unlocking, flashing, recovery and troubleshooting |

## Verdict

Custom ROMs are still worth it in 2026, but for different reasons than in 2016. Back then, stock Android was limited and often slow, and a custom ROM was the main way to get a good experience. Today stock is good, so the case for flashing rests on what stock cannot give you: updates after the maker stops, control over what Google collects, deeper customization and root. If none of those matters to you, the stock phone is the better phone.

Flash a custom ROM if you:

- Value privacy genuinely (not just in theory)
- Own a device with expired software support
- Want customization beyond what stock offers
- Enjoy the tinkering aspect
- Want root access for its specific benefits

Stay on stock if you:

- Camera quality is your top priority
- You want zero maintenance and maximum convenience
- Banking apps and payments can’t have any hiccups
- You don’t have time to troubleshoot issues

If you are undecided, a phone whose official updates have already ended is the best place to try a ROM: there is little to lose and the most to gain.

A ROM (historically "read-only memory") is simply the Android operating system image that runs your phone. Stock firmware is the OEM build — Google's Pixel software, Samsung's One UI, and so on — signed by the manufacturer and locked down by default. A custom ROM is an alternative build, usually based on the Android Open Source Project (AOSP), that you install in place of the stock image.

To flash one you normally unlock the bootloader: the low-level code that decides which software is allowed to boot. That single act is the root of every trade-off here — it enables custom software, and it also breaks the manufacturer's chain of trust. Unlocking the bootloader wipes the entire device, so a full backup first is non-negotiable. In practice, custom ROM vs stock is really a question of how much of that trust chain you're willing to swap for control.

## Custom ROM vs stock: the honest comparison

Here's how the two stack up across the factors that matter day to day. There's no universal winner — only the right fit for your device and habits.

| Factor | Stock Android | Custom ROM |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Privacy & telemetry | Google/OEM services baked in | De-Googled options minimise tracking |
| Bloatware | Carrier/OEM apps, often unremovable | Clean AOSP base; install only what you want |
| Update lifespan | Ends when the OEM drops support | Community builds extend older devices for years |
| Customisation | Limited to OEM settings | Themes, granular permissions, optional root |
| Banking & Play Integrity | Passes hardware-backed checks | Often passes basic/device, rarely STRONG |
| Wallet & tap-to-pay | Works | Frequently breaks once unlocked |
| Warranty & OTA | Intact; automatic updates | May void warranty; updates need more hands-on care |
| Security model | Locked bootloader, verified boot | GrapheneOS hardens; most others weaken verified boot |
| Effort & risk | None | Real bricking risk; needs patience |
| Device choice | Any phone | Only unlockable, supported models |

...

People ask "why install a custom ROM" for four practical reasons:

- Privacy and de-Googling. Builds like LineageOS (optionally without Google apps) and GrapheneOS strip out the always-on telemetry that ships with most stock firmware.
- A longer life for your phone. When the manufacturer stops issuing patches, the community often carries on, keeping hardware secure and useful well past its official end date.
- No bloatware. You start from a clean base and add only the apps you actually use.
- Genuine control. Granular permissions, theming and the option to root for deeper tweaks.

...

## Why stock Android still wins for some people

Stock isn't the "boring" choice — for many people it's the correct one. It keeps:

- Verified boot and hardware-backed security, with the bootloader locked and the trust chain intact.
- Reliable banking, wallet and tap-to-pay, because the device passes Google's strictest attestation.
- DRM playback at full resolution (Widevine L1) for streaming apps.
- Warranty and effortless OTA updates that arrive automatically.

If your phone is your bank card, your transit pass and your work device all at once, the convenience of stock can outweigh everything a custom ROM offers.

## The 2026 catch: Play Integrity and attestation

This is the single biggest reason switching is harder than it used to be. Google retired the old SafetyNet system in 2024 and replaced it with the Play Integrity API, which apps use to check whether a device is "genuine". It returns three verdicts: MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY, MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY and the hardware-backed MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY.

In practice, a rooted or bootloader-unlocked device reliably passes only BASIC, and often DEVICE once you add the community "Play Integrity Fix" module — but STRONG, which is anchored in the phone's secure hardware, is effectively off the table once you unlock. Some banking and wallet apps demand STRONG; many don't. We can't promise any method will satisfy a specific bank's checks, and what works can change with any app update.

Unlike the stock Android experience that comes installed on your phone, these alternative versions are made by independent developers and the wider community of Android users. They offer features, performance improvements, and customization options that would otherwise be unavailable. Since Android is an open-source operating system, its core code is freely available. Developers can rebuild and modify the OS from the ground up, adding unique features, optimizing performance, or even bringing the latest Android version to older devices. This process replaces proprietary components from device manufacturers with community-developed alternatives that often prioritize user control, privacy, and performance. ### Stability issues

 Android ROMs may lead to bugs and stability problems that affect daily usability, even if it’s not immediately apparent. Newly released ROMs or experimental features might cause random reboots, app crashes, or hardware malfunctions that rarely occur with stock firmware. Banking apps, payment systems, or other kinds of sensitive content frequently detect custom ROMs and block user access, limiting your device’s usefulness for some basic tasks. 

### Security weaknesses

 Custom ROM users have to actively monitor for updates and security patches since they won’t get any automatic updates from their phone’s manufacturer. The thing is, building custom Android ROMs is tough work. Many ROMs are maintained by a single developer, so fixing bugs and keeping up with security updates are often challenging. More popular ROMs tend to get timely updates, but there’s a good chance more niche projects will lag behind. Even if you’re always looking out for patches, your device is still more vulnerable to new threats. 

### Incompatible software

 Many apps include features that rely on proprietary components that come from the device manufacturer. A custom ROM may be incompatible with some of these features. Things like advanced camera modes or fingerprint sensors might not work properly with customer ROMs that lack access to closed-source drivers or proprietary software. 

### Bricking risks

 Device bricking is the most serious risk you can face when tinkering with your Android operating system. In simple terms, bricking is when you accidentally make your device completely unusable. By incorrectly installing a custom ROM or adding incompatible firmware, you may make your phone non-functional — for good. Some “soft bricks” can be recovered through fastboot mode or custom recovery tools, but “hard bricks” often require professional repair or result in permanent device loss. Think you’re under warranty? Think again. Unlocking your bootloader typically voids manufacturer warranties. So user beware — adding AOSP ROMs carries the very real risk of you losing your Android.

 Instead of installing a custom add-on, you can stick with the stock ROM that came preinstalled on your Android. This lets you improve your device’s look and functionality without completely replacing the operating system. Today, leading manufacturers offer much better customization options than they did even a few years ago, so making thoughtful, minimal changes to your Android with apps and widgets might be all the personalization you need. - Designed to have regular updates and fewer bugs.

You cannot install just any custom ROM on any Android device. [1] The ROM must match your exact model, codename, and carrier variant. [2] 

### Essential Prerequisites

Your bootloader must be unlockable. [2] [3] You also need a custom recovery such as TWRP or the ROM's own recovery. [1] [2] 

### Required Tools

Install the latest Android SDK Platform Tools (ADB and Fastboot) on your computer. [2] Download USB drivers for your device. [2] A good USB cable is essential. [1] 

### Enable Developer Options

Go to Settings, find About Phone, and tap Build Number seven times. [1] [2] This unlocks Developer Options.

### Turn On Necessary Settings

In Developer Options, enable OEM unlocking (if available) and USB debugging. [1] [2] You may need to enter your lock screen password. [1] 

### Back Up Your Device

Create a full backup using TWRP or other tools before wiping data. [2] [3] Back up your special partition (EFS, PDS, etc.) to preserve IMEI and connectivity. [2] 

## Unlocking the Bootloader

Connect your phone to your computer and open a command prompt in the platform-tools folder. [1] [2] 

### Basic Commands

Run 'adb devices' to confirm connection, then 'adb reboot bootloader' to enter fastboot mode. [1] [2] 

### Unlock Command

Enter 'fastboot flashing unlock' or 'fastboot oem unlock' depending on your device. [1] [2] Confirm on the phone screen using volume and power buttons. [1]

Download the TWRP image for your exact device from the official TWRP site. [2] 

### Flashing TWRP

With your device in bootloader mode, run 'fastboot flash recovery twrp.img' or 'fastboot boot twrp.img'. [1] [2]

Some devices require 'fastboot flash boot recovery.img' followed by 'fastboot reboot recovery'. [1] Boot into recovery by holding the correct button combination during reboot. [2]

Copy the ZIP files to your device's internal storage or prepare to sideload them via ADB. [1] [2]

Enter recovery mode, then perform a factory reset or full Format Data when switching ROMs. [2] [3] Avoid wiping persist, modem, or EFS partitions. [3] 

### Install via Recovery

Select Install, choose the ROM ZIP, and swipe to flash. [2] Immediately flash GApps if required, before rebooting. [1] [2] 

### ADB Sideload Method

In recovery, enable ADB sideload and run 'adb sideload rom.zip' from your computer. [1] [3] Repeat for GApps and other add-ons. [1]

Complete the setup wizard after the first boot. [3] Check that Wi-Fi, calls, camera, and sensors work. [3]

Published Oct 23, 2026, 1:00 PM EDT
I've been writing about Android since 2011, with a focus on device reviews, Samsung and Google Pixel hardware, and the latest happenings in the ecosystem. In my entire writing career, I've reviewed more than 75 Android phones.
Carrying both a Samsung or Pixel flagship and an iPhone as a daily driver provides me with deep insight into how Android works and how it compares to iOS.

When not working, I tend to mindlessly scroll through X, play with new AI models, or go on long road trips. You can reach out to me on X or drop a mail at rajesh@androidpolice.com.
I had not tried custom ROMs in eight or nine years, so LineageOS's new browser-based flashing tool gave me a good excuse to see how things have evolved.
I had grown bored with the stock Pixel UI on the Google Pixel 8 Pro and wanted to see what custom ROMs offered in 2026.
Google's software provides a clean Android experience, at least on the Pixel. Yet LineageOS felt surprisingly bloat-free, though I had to dig around to find its most useful customization options.
### Even Google's software felt busy by comparison
Installing LineageOS on my Google Pixel 8 Pro required some preparation. Thankfully, the detailed, device-specific wiki instructions made the process easier, while the browser-based flash tool saved setup time.
After the first boot, the clean interface and small number of preinstalled apps surprised me most. I wasn't switching from One UI or ColorOS, which ship with a plethora of duplicate apps and promotional notifications.
I was coming from Pixel UI, Google's take on Android, which has a reputation for being clean. Yet, I was surprised by how clean LineageOS felt on my Pixel 8 Pro.
That's largely because it doesn't include Google's usual suite of preinstalled apps. Instead, you must flash the relevant GApps package, which installs only the basic apps and services.
During initial setup, the ROM prompted me to select which additional Google apps I wanted to install.
I prefer this approach over having unwanted apps — even if they are from Google — on my phone.
My Pixel 8 Pro also felt smoother to navigate, though I wouldn't give LineageOS all the credit for it. Its under-the-hood optimizations must play a role, but I can't discount the effect of a clean install without my usual collection of apps and accumulated data.
By Irene Okpanachi
### The default apps deserve a second look
Back in the day, LineageOS and other custom ROMs weren't exactly known for their bundled apps. They often felt like they were there to cover the basics. But that's no longer the case.
With LineageOS 24, the team refreshed several of its bundled apps to use Material Design 3 Expressive, giving them a modern look and feel. It also added Canvas, an image editor featuring tools for cropping, adjusting white balance, and applying filters.
Even the bundled Glimpse gallery and Aperture camera apps have improved, with a polished UI and more than just the basics. I still defaulted to my preferred apps, including Google Photos, but the bundled LineageOS apps are now better than before, and you don't need a replacement for everyday use.
Since I run my own Jellyfin server, Twelve's Jellyfin support — the stock music player on LineageOS — makes streaming my music collection easy.

At first glance, LineageOS seemed to offer a cleaner Pixel UI experience. But as I started using the ROM and dug deeper into the settings menu, I discovered several useful options.

LineageOS's battery information menu reported my Pixel 8 Pro's battery health capacity at 95% and charging cycle count at 228. Those figures help me decide whether it's time to replace the battery.

GrapheneOS maximizes security hardening while keeping app compatibility through sandboxed Google Play. The real risks surround it: an unlocked bootloader weakens verified boot and some theft protection, unofficial builds go unreviewed, wrong firmware can brick a phone, banking apps may refuse to run, and patch speed varies by ROM.

...

For an official build from a maintained project, the ROM is rarely the weak point. Projects such as LineageOS and crDroid publish their source code openly, build each device’s release themselves, and host it on their own download server or project page. LineageOS also signs its builds, and its install pages say that if the recovery reports a signature failure, the file “is either corrupted, or not an official LineageOS image”. That chain (public source, a named maintainer, an official host, a signature) is what makes an official build trustworthy, and it is also what an unofficial build or a re-upload on a file-sharing site lacks. This is why every download link on this site goes only to the hosts each project publishes its own builds on, checked against an exact list of hosts, so a lookalike domain or a file pushed to a copy of a project’s repository is never linked. Whether a build is safe to download depends far more on where it came from than on which ROM it is. Our ROM directory links each project’s official site and source.

## What does unlocking the bootloader change?

Unlocking the bootloader is the biggest real security change a custom ROM brings, because it switches off the check that keeps unapproved software from starting. Android’s Verified Boot documentation says the feature “strives to ensure all executed code comes from a trusted source (usually device OEMs), rather than from an attacker or corruption”. Android’s device state page explains the trade: “LOCKED devices boot only if the loaded OS is properly signed by the root of trust”, while “UNLOCKED devices allow modification”. Anyone who holds an unlocked phone can therefore flash different software to it, which is why every lock state change wipes the data partitions “to protect user data”. The orange warning you see on every boot afterwards says exactly this; Android’s boot flow page words it as “The bootloader is unlocked and software integrity cannot be guaranteed.” Some brands also switch features off. Xiaomi’s Mi Unlock page says features that need a high security level, “e.g., Find device”, “will no longer be available” once unlocked. On Samsung phones, the Knox FAQ says a non-Knox bootloader or kernel trips a one-time e-fuse, after which Samsung Pay and Secure Folder stop working, and “there is no way to revert” it. Our bootloader unlocking guide covers each brand.

## Why are unofficial builds riskier?

An unofficial build is any build not made and published by the project itself, and the risk is that nobody accountable has reviewed it. Plenty of unofficial builds are made in good faith by someone porting a ROM to a phone the project does not support, but you cannot tell a careful port from a tampered file by its name, and the project cannot either. LineageOS says in its FAQ that it only provides help for officially supported devices, and that moving from an unofficial build to an official one means following “the installation guide for your device exactly as written”, data format included. Unofficial builds also tend to stop. When the person who made one moves on, the security patches stop with them, often with no notice on the page where you downloaded it. If you do install one, prefer a build whose source is public and whose maker is identifiable, download it from where they announced it rather than a mirror, and check its patch date regularly. If your phone has an official build of any maintained ROM, that is the safer starting point; its device page on this site lists them.

...

Yes, and of all the ways a custom ROM install can go wrong, this is the one that can leave a phone that will not start at all. Firmware is the set of device-specific images, such as the bootloader and modem, that the manufacturer’s software updates and a custom ROM depends on. LineageOS install pages ask for a specific firmware version per phone and warn that the wrong one “may result in failure to install LineageOS, unexpected crashes post-installation, or permanent damage to your device”. Some phones add rollback protection on top. Android’s Verified Boot documentation says it exists to keep an exploit from becoming persistent “by ensuring devices only update to newer versions of Android”, and on some phones flashing firmware older than what the phone already ran is how that protection turns a mistake into a brick. The practical rule is to install exactly the firmware your ROM’s instructions name for your model and region, and nothing older. Our LineageOS install guide and crDroid install guide show where those requirements are published, and the unbrick guide covers recovery when it goes wrong.

## Will banking and payment apps still work?

Some will and some will not, and the reason is Google’s Play Integrity API rather than anything unsafe about the ROM. Apps can ask Play Integrity for a verdict about the device. Google’s verdict documentation defines three levels. `MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY` allows a bootloader that is “locked or unlocked”. `MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY` requires, on Android 13 and higher, “hardware-backed proof that the device bootloader is locked and the loaded Android OS is a certified device manufacturer image”. `MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY` adds security updates “in the last year for all partitions of the device”. A phone running a custom ROM on an unlocked bootloader cannot honestly meet the second or third level, so an app that demands them will refuse to run, however secure the ROM is. Projects respond differently. LineageOS says in its FAQ that it does not remove the unlock and verity flags, “as it isn’t our place to lie about security features”. Check the apps you cannot live without before you unlock, and read our Play Integrity guide for what is and is not possible.

...

It varies by ROM, by device and by maintainer, and the only reliable answer is the patch date on the build you actually run. A custom ROM gets Android’s monthly security fixes by merging Google’s published patches into its source and releasing a new build for each phone, so its patch level always trails Google’s bulletin by some amount. LineageOS describes the layers in its FAQ: Android platform patches, which it “integrates, tests, and ships … for all supported devices as quickly as possible”; the vendor security patch level, which “reflects the patch level of the stock firmware your device’s vendor blobs were taken from”; and firmware such as the bootloader and modem, which it “cannot update … on its own”. That last part matters for old phones. Once the manufacturer stops updating a model, no ROM can fix its closed vendor components, whatever the platform patch date says. To check a build, open Settings > About phone and find the Android security update or patch level, then compare it with Google’s Android Security Bulletins. Our security patch tip shows the ADB commands for both dates.

## How do you keep the risk low?

Each risk on this page has a matching habit, and none of them needs special tools or knowledge beyond reading the instructions carefully. Download only official builds, from the host the project itself names, and match the codename and model exactly. Install the firmware the instructions name, not an older one. Use the recovery the ROM’s instructions name, follow the install page line by line, and stop if a step fails rather than improvising. Keep the phone updated after install, because an unpatched custom ROM is worse than the stock software it replaced. Set a strong screen lock, since an unlocked bootloader makes physical access more valuable to a thief. Check whether your bank, payment and work apps need Play Integrity before you unlock, not after. Do not relock the bootloader over a custom ROM unless the project documents it; the LineageOS FAQ warns that relocking “can result in actual unusable devices”. And keep a backup, because unlocking and clean flashing both wipe the phone and a backup is the only way back. New to all of this? Start with getting started with custom ROMs.

Highlights:
There are a number of reasons why it can be a good idea to install an alternative operating system (aka. Custom ROM) on an Android device: better performance, more privacy, longer security updates and of course customization. Whatever the reason may be, users of custom ROMs (including myself) usually struggle with the fact that many banking apps and other “high security” apps refuse to run on rooted devices.

In this post I will share how I managed to work around this issue. We’ll go over installing LineageOS with Google Apps, installing Magisk and PlayIntegrityFix module, configuring Magisk DenyList to hide root and finally testing the setup with the Play Integrity API Checker. For reference, I’m using LineageOS 20 (Android 13) on a Motorola Moto G7 Plus (`lake`). I got the apps `DKB`, `Revolut`, `SAP Concur` as well as `Google Wallet` working with this approach.

## # Install PlayIntegrityFix

PlayIntegrityFix is a Magisk module that hooks into the Play Integrity and SafetyNet frameworks (provided by Google Play Services) and make them return accepted values.

On the phone, download the latest ZIP from the releases page and install via the “Modules” tab at the bottom of the Magisk App, then reboot once again.

## # Testing

At this point we need to check the basic functionality, for which we can use a special app called Play Integrity API Checker that should be installed from the Google Play Store.

This should return:

```

3

```

```sh
MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY: OK
MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY: OK
MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY: FAILED

```

Due to the fact that the bootloader is unlocked, we can’t pass the `MEETS_STRONG_INTEGRITY` check, but that’s not necessary for most use cases. The important ones are the `MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY` and `MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY` checks.

At this point, most financial apps as well as Google Wallet should be working.

## # Hide Magisk

Some apps implement additional, custom checks for the device they run on. To trick these apps into working, we need to “hide” the fact that the phone has root capabilties. Thanks to Magisk’s powerful capabilities, this is possible with the built-in DenyList feature. Open up the Magisk app, click on the Settings icon in the top-right corner, scroll down and enable the Zygisk and Enforce DenyList options.

Then configure the DenyList as follows:

- check Android Services Library
- check any other app that you want to hide root capabilities from (in my case DKB)

If this is still not enough, you may also want to try to rename the Magisk app (see Settings > MagiskHide).

Finally, it’s a good idea to clear the local storage of the app we are trying to hide from. This ensures that the previous “bad” state is not persisted across restarts. Now the app should work even though we a custom ROM with root!

## The short answer

Whether you can make a banking app work depends on which check it uses. Apps that only look for signs of root on the phone can often be satisfied. Apps that require Play Integrity's DEVICE or STRONG verdict on Android 13 or newer cannot, while the bootloader is unlocked.

- DEVICE / STRONG, Android 13+ Fails Needs hardware proof of a locked bootloader
- Google Wallet tap to pay Not supported Google lists rooted and unlocked phones

...

- The app's own checks are written by the bank or its security vendor. They look for the Magisk app's package, an `su` binary, unusual mounts, or hooking frameworks such as LSPosed (Vector). This is where the DenyList and hiding modules help.
- Play Integrity is Google's service. The app asks Google for a verdict and gets labels back. By default an app receives only `MEETS_DEVICE_INTEGRITY` or nothing; BASIC and STRONG are labels it opts in to. On Android 13 and newer, Google says DEVICE integrity requires "hardware-backed proof that the device bootloader is locked". The verdicts are explained on Play Integrity and root.
- App and environment signals are optional extras an app can ask Play Integrity for: whether you installed the app from Google Play, the Play Protect status, and whether apps that can capture the screen, show overlays or control the device are running.

1. Get the Magisk app out of sight. Since v31.1, the current stable release, the release notes recommend simply uninstalling the Magisk app once your root grants and modules are set up; root and modules keep working without it. On v30.7 and older, Hide the Magisk app in the app's settings reinstalls it under a random package name instead.
2. Turn on Zygisk and add the app to the DenyList. In Magisk's settings, enable Zygisk, open Configure DenyList, and tick the bank app, including all of its processes. With Enforce DenyList on, Magisk reverts its mounts in those processes, and its source shows that no Zygisk modules are loaded into them either. More in Zygisk and the DenyList.
3. If that isn't enough, try a hiding module. Magisk's FAQ says Magisk no longer hides root and leaves that to modules. All three have had no new release for over a year (see the module catalog), so results vary.

- If the app requires Play Integrity DEVICE or STRONG on Android 13 or newer, hiding root does not help. The verdict depends on the bootloader state reported by hardware, not on what is installed.

Highlights:
I run stock LineageOS without GApps. microG handles the Play Services replacement. Most apps work fine on this setup. Banking apps and anything that calls Google's Play Integrity API do not, at least not without a stack of community modules and one specific microG toggle that defaults to "block".

Can a Google-free Android still pass Play Integrity well enough for banking apps?

Short answer: yes, DEVICE-grade, on a custom ROM with an unlocked bootloader. It takes a leaked keybox, the right modules, and one toggle off. I spent a long evening getting Revolut, Erste George, McDonald's, and the rest of the Aurora-installed proprietary apps to work on this device. Here is what mattered and what was a dead end.

...

## The one toggle#

microG `0.3.9` added a setting called Block hardware attestation under Device Attestation -> Advanced. It defaults to on. Most "I tried microG, banking apps don't work" guides stop right there.

When this is on, microG's `DroidGuard` re-implementation refuses to forward hardware-attestation requests to Google's Play Integrity API. The verdict path returns `MEETS_BASIC_INTEGRITY` at best. That is why every guide on the internet says microG can't pass DEVICE integrity. Banking apps that require DEVICE, which is most of them now, show their flavour of "this device cannot be trusted".

Turn it off, reboot, and microG produces DEVICE-grade integrity tokens when the rest of your stack is set up right. I found it nowhere in the first dozen pages of search results. It is buried in a `microg/GmsCore` GitHub issue with 72 comments going back to mid-2025, in a reply from the maintainer.

...

## The keybox economy#

Hardware-backed Play Integrity wants the device to sign an attestation challenge with a key chained to Google's Hardware Attestation Root CA. A real phone with a working TEE produces this naturally. A custom ROM with an unlocked bootloader cannot, the bootloader unlock broke the chain.

The workaround is a leaked OEM keybox. Someone extracted a real per-device attestation key from a real phone (Samsung Knox, Pixel TEE, MediaTek, the OEM doesn't matter much). The private key plus its full certificate chain ends up in an XML file called `keybox.xml`. You drop that file in `/data/adb/tricky_store/keybox.xml`. A module called `TEESimulator` (the successor to the dormant `Tricky Store`) intercepts the Android Keystore API calls, signs the attestation challenge with the leaked key, and returns the leaked chain.

```text
App asks for integrity verdict
        |
        v
Android Keystore attestation  -->  TEESimulator intercepts
        |                                  |
        |                          signs with leaked key,
        |                          returns leaked chain
        v                                  v
Google verifier checks chain against Hardware Attestation Root CA
        |
        +-- leaf serial NOT on CRL  -->  DEVICE
        +-- leaf serial on CRL      -->  BASIC, back to weekly rotation

...

Google checks the chain, doesn't notice (or doesn't care) that the same per-device key is in use across thousands of devices, and returns DEVICE. It does eventually notice. Every leaked keybox lands on Google's certificate revocation list at `https://android.googleapis.com/attestation/status`, and verifiers check that list. The window between "leaked keybox shows up in a community feed" and "Google revokes the leaf serial" runs 6 to 31 days based on the historical data I looked at.
